name: dungeon
why: The original Zork-lineage text adventure from MIT, a piece of computing history worth an afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: DUNGEON is a classic text adventure game, the original program that became the basis for the Zork series. This repository is a version 4.0 update of Robert Supnik's 1980 VAX FORTRAN port, changed so it compiles with gfortran. You type text commands at the prompt and the game prints text responses. The game needs its 'dindx' and 'dtext' data files in the working directory when you run the 'dungeon' executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the original source depended on a nonstandard VAX FORTRAN extension that modern Fortran compilers no longer support. The update exists to make DUNGEON compile with gfortran, 'enabling a new generation of adventurers to "GET LAMP."'
brief.how_it_works: The original game was written in MDL on a DEC PDP-10 at MIT in the late 1970s, then ported to VAX FORTRAN in 1980. This repo keeps most of Supnik's source and makes the changes needed for gfortran. The README says there are no functional differences from Supnik's late-1994 V3.2B release.

commands_seen.context: Run from the src directory to build the dungeon executable with gfortran and make installed.

brief.install_notes: Requires gfortran and make. Build by running make from the src directory. The resulting dungeon executable must be run from the directory that contains the dindx and dtext files. Older compilers such as g77 are untested and may not compile it. No accounts or other setup are mentioned.
brief.standout: This is the original 1977-80 MIT game with its source kept largely intact, so the port is a compatibility update rather than a rewrite. It keeps the game's history visible, and the author's note that it preserves V3.2B behaviour makes it a faithful copy of the original.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows version V.4.0 and cites a late-1994 V3.2B baseline, but gives no release date, last commit date, or maintenance note. I could not tell whether the project is active.
brief.caveats: The license is for non-commercial use only. Only gfortran with make is documented; g77 is untested. The executable must be run from the directory holding dindx and dtext, or it will not find its data. The README gives no build-status or platform notes beyond that.

entry.title: dungeon
entry.tldr: The original MIT text adventure that became Zork, in Robert Supnik's 1980 FORTRAN port, updated so it builds with gfortran today.
entry.deeper_look:
DUNGEON is a text adventure. You type commands at a prompt, such as looking around, taking objects and opening doors, and the game prints prose back. It began as a program written in MDL on a DEC PDP-10 at MIT in the late 1970s, and it is the game the Zork series grew out of. In 1980 Robert Supnik ported it to VAX FORTRAN.

This repository is a version 4.0 update of that port. The original source depended on a nonstandard VAX FORTRAN extension that modern compilers no longer support. The update changes only what gfortran needs, so the code stays close to Supnik's. The README says there are no functional differences from his late-1994 V3.2B release. Its stated aim is "enabling a new generation of adventurers to 'GET LAMP.'"

The game is a way into early interactive fiction. The source is old, readable FORTRAN, so you can play the game and then read how a 1980 program parsed commands and stored its world and text. The data lives in two files, dindx and dtext, which the executable reads at startup.
entry.install:
brew install dungeon
# Homebrew builds it with gcc. Run it from the directory that holds the dindx and dtext data files, or it will not find them.

try_this.what_happens: Runs the listed executable with a help flag. The brief does not document flags, so the game may simply start. Run it from the directory with dindx and dtext.
Only if you build from source: run it in the repo's src directory to build the dungeon executable. It needs gfortran and make.

entry.whats_unique: It is the original 1977-80 MIT game with its source largely intact, not a rewrite or a clone. The port is a compatibility update, so the history stays visible.
entry.caveats: The license is non-commercial use only, the README gives no release or maintenance dates, and the game must be run from the directory containing dindx and dtext.
